content.thinking:
I'm planning the full build in one pass to keep it correct from the start, designing a whimsical low-poly gnome around 1.1m tall with faceted rounded forms. I'm laying out the skeleton structure—hips as root, spine, chest, neck, head, jaw, arms, and legs with full joint chains.

Working through exact coordinates and joint spans for hips, spine, neck, and head, double-checking that the number of names matches the span count for each catmull chain so the hierarchy builds correctly.

Simplifying to two spine names for two spans, so chest is the final span joint aimed at the path end, and neck parents off that. Then I'm setting up head and jaw joints with explicit positions and aim directions so the head faces forward while the bone points mostly upward, and starting to size a sphere-like head shape.

Now I'm placing the facial features: a rounded nose bulb, eye spheres with pupils, bushy eyebrows, and a layered white beard made from stacked cones hanging off the chin, plus mustache capsules and a small lower-lip piece on the jaw bone.

For the hat, I'm shaping a tall tilted pointy cone with a brim, a bent tip, plus a band, buckle, and goggles with glowing teal lenses sitting on top, along with pointy ear cones on the sides of the head. Then I'm moving on to sketching out the torso as a swept spine shape for the body.

Working out where to attach the apron extrusion relative to the torso's tapering radius, settling on placing it around z 0.16 with some embedding thickness to sit flush against the belly curve.

For the belt, I'm planning a closed ring sweep of 8 points around the hips at radius 0.18 with tube thickness 0.02, slightly larger than the torso radius there, plus a brass buckle box centered at the front. Then for the arms, I'm setting shoulder anchor points symmetrically at x=±0.19 and sketching an A-pose path using a catmull curve from shoulder outward and down.

Continuing the arm chain, I'm defining the shoulder-elbow-wrist points with decreasing radii for a tapered limb, naming them by side (L for +X, R for -X) and parenting to the chest joint, with sleeve coloring and a sphere hand capping each wrist.

I'll keep the hand simple: a palm sphere with a thumb bump, skipping individual fingers, and instead tuck a wrench into the belt for a hand prop. For the legs, I'm placing hip, knee, and ankle joints down the side and connecting them as a polyline chain.

Still working out leg proportions and boot geometry...

Confirmed midpoint subdivision gives exact poles, so I'll just use a simple sphere geometry with enough segments instead of worrying about icosahedron math. Now I'm sketching the boot shape as a scaled sphere part, positioning it so the bottom sits flush at the ground, and starting to shape a pointy curled toe cap.

Still placing boot parts... I'm also thinking through the bone rig — using the ankle joint tip from the leg chain as the foot attachment point — and sketching out a backpack as a simple box frame attached to the chest bone, positioned on the back.

Now I'm shaping the backpack's top flap and shoulder straps as curved sweep paths running from the pack down to the chest, using small cross-section radii so they look like proper fabric straps.

I'll accept the torso's rounded cap overlapping the neck slightly since the beard will hide it, and adjust the strap points so their radius at each height matches the dome curve of the torso cap.

Working out the spine path for torso and neck, I'm placing shoulders at y 0.62 with the torso tapering to a rounded top, then the neck segment running from there up to a small head at y 0.92 with radius 0.15 — though I'm noticing the neck radius might leave a visible gap at that length.

Head bottom at 0.77 lines up fine against torso top at 0.75. Now I'm defining the head as a scaled sphere positioned at [0,0.93,0.05], and working out the hat geometry sitting above it — a tilted cone brim starting at y 1.04 with its own height, radius, and tip direction computed from a normalized vector.

I'm realizing the second cone's base radius will leave a floating disc where it meets the first cone's pointed tip, so instead I'm switching both cones to tapered frustums (cylinder geometry with different top/bottom radii) to avoid that gap, setting up the dimensions for the first frustum now.

For the hat coloring, I'm thinking of adding a red base with cream spots using the existing paint system, which should work fine on the cone parts since they share the same 3D coordinate painting approach as the rest of the model.

Adding brim and band...

Working out goggle rim and glass lens positions on the hat front, then placing the eyes beneath the brim so they peek out above the head's front curve, using small white spheres for the eyes with pupils to follow.

Still placing facial features...

Adding the mouth detail under the mustache, then shaping the pointy ears with skin-colored cones, and setting up a limited color palette for skin, nose, hat, and tunic tones.

Now rounding out the palette with leather, brass, steel, glow, and gadget colors to keep the count manageable, then starting the backpack body as a leather box positioned at the chest.

Adding pack details...

Placing the gear flat in the XY plane on the pack's back face, no extra rotation needed since it's symmetric from both sides. Still planning other mechanical details -- a lathe-built funnel on the side, copper tube sweeps with small valve wheels connecting pack to side, and a pressure gauge made from a circular disc with an SVG dial texture (face and needle) oriented outward on the back.

I'm also sketching a wrench accessory: a steel rod handle with an open-end jaw head, built as an extruded 2D outline mounted vertically on the pack's back, defining the handle and jaw notch points in meters.

I'll keep the asymmetrical notch shape as-is rather than forcing symmetry, confirming the path winds counter-clockwise without self-crossing. Then I'll extrude it with a slight thickness and bevel, position it along the right axes, and give it a steel color so it reads correctly from both sides.

Now I'm adding the hammer accessory: a brown wooden rod handle with a boxy head, hung vertically on the pack's side, plus a hanging lantern at the back with a glowing glass box and brass fittings.

Then I'm placing clockwork gadgets across the back face -- a brass gauge, a large brass gear, a smaller interlocking steel gear, and a wrench positioned on the lower left so it overlaps a bit with the gauge above it.

Adding the pack top details next—flap, buckle, telescope, antenna, a dangling tin cup with handle, a glowing potion bottle in the right pouch, leather side pouches, and a horizontal bedroll cylinder along the bottom rotated to lie flat.

I'm resolving the item placement conflicts: bedroll sits under the pack, lantern hangs from the right side with a rope, and the hammer stays on the left (negative x) to balance the potion pouch on the right.

I'm untangling the hammer and wrench overlap at the back, mug placement, and belt attachments by shifting the wrench to the back-right and dropping the hammer to avoid clashing with other hanging gear.

I'm also adding a mounted coil spring made with a spiral sweep on top of the pack, working out the radius and pitch parameters to get a convincing coiled shape among the other props like gauges, gears, pipes, and lantern.

Still routing the copper pipe geometry...

Now I'm adding a small lathe-generated funnel attached to the top of the pack, shaping its conical outline from a narrow neck to a flared opening.

Checking the other edge confirms no crossing, so the shape is fine with no smoothing and 8 segments. Now I'm thinking about the pack's moving parts — assigning them to the chest joint on the spine, and deciding which features should be hinged, like the flap lid and propeller, while skipping extras like a telescope or goggles lens.

Working out the flap hinge placement at the back top edge of the pack, oriented so it opens forward, with the lid box sized and positioned accordingly, plus adding straps and a buckle at the front of the flap.

Now I'm adding a rotor assembly on top: a mast rising from the chest, a hinge joint for rotation, and two flat blade boxes set at 90 degrees to each other with slight pitch, capped with a sphere, colored red and cream for a whimsical touch.

For extra charm I'm sticking a small flower in the hat band with a green stem rod and a ring of yellow petals around an orange center. Then I'm deciding to give the whole figure a lowpoly faceted look by disabling smoothing on the sweep geometry for the tunic and limbs, keeping the skin smooth for contrast.

Now I'm working out color palettes: a teal-and-cream horizontal-striped shirt under mustard-brown overalls, with a red hat, applying the same stripe pattern along the world y-axis to the sleeves so the bands stay consistent across the diagonal arms.

For the pants, I'm giving the mustard overalls a mottled texture for subtle variation and adding a small decal patch on the right knee as a cream square positioned at the knee joint for a stitched-patch detail.

Now I'm shaping the bib of the overalls as an extruded leather outline across the torso, sizing it to taper from wider at the belt to narrower near the chest, matching it against the torso's curvature so it sits flush against the body rather than floating off the surface.

Working out the cross product for the bib's thickness direction so it points outward correctly, landing on a reasonable z-offset at the belly front. Now I'm positioning the pocket and brass buttons at the bib's top corners using the local coordinate transform.

Adding stitched pocket outline using thin cream boxes, then placing a belt loop above the bib with a radius that clears the torso curve, checking that belt and bib vertical ranges fit together properly on the torso's keyed radius profile.

I'm working through the hip spine path and realizing the torso's rounded bottom cap extends lower than the leg attachment point, which gives a fuller pants-like silhouette, so I'm considering coloring that bottom dome to match the pants rather than the torso.

I decide to use a band-based sweep where the lower portion gets the pants color and the rest shirt color, placing the belt at the transition point to visually hide the seam. Checking that the floor contact at the boots is fine and the torso bottom stays above ground, I move on to defining the leg joints from hip to knee.

Still defining leg geometry...

Placing arm joint coordinates next, defining shoulder, elbow, and wrist positions with tapering radii, then adding a cream cuff band near the wrist oriented along the forearm direction.

For the hands, I'm scaling a sphere at the wrist with tan work-glove coloring, then adding a thumb capsule and four finger capsules extending from the hand center along the forearm direction with slight lateral offsets to simulate a relaxed, slightly curled grip.

I'll simplify finger rigging to one "fingers" joint and one "thumb" joint per hand rather than full joint chains, keeping it at four joints total. Then I'm planning the rod helper function for capsule-shaped bone segments, and deciding to skip eyelids since brows should be sufficient for the face.

For hair, I'm sketching white tufts peeking from under the hat using spike shapes, skipping sideburns since the beard covers that area. For beard detail I'm considering scattering small fur-like card textures across the beard cone's surface using a tuft SVG shape.

Writing tuft SVG markup...

Now I'm thinking through how the cards should be oriented—flow pointing downward, leaning around 70 degrees so the fibers lie flat along the cone's surface, while also checking which way the cone's normals point near the apex to make sure the fur reads correctly as it tapers.

Moving to the mustache next, I'm sweeping a catmull curve with a tapering capsule radius to form it, then binding it to the head joint. I'm also writing a gear geometry helper that builds a cylinder body and will add teeth around its edge, handling optional center holes.

Adding a bolt cylinder for the hub, and sketching the gauge's brass rim cylinder rotated to sit flat along the z-axis.

Now I'm placing the gauge face as a small textured dial disc behind the rim, positioning it slightly deeper in z so it reads correctly. I'm also sketching a lantern on the side with a brass cap, glowing glass box, and a base, hung by a rope from a hook on the pack.

Still placing accessories...

Repositioning the propeller mast and telescope to avoid overlap, moving the mast to z -.28 and telescope to z -.18. Adjusting the rotor height and blade dimensions so the propeller clears the hat tip near the head.

Now I'm placing a coil spring on the lid between the mast and telescope, then adding a small side-mounted crank to the gear hub with a short rod and knob at the end.

Finishing the crank's lever arm with a knob at the top, then positioning a blue bedroll cylinder under the pack with brown strap bands, checking it sits flush against the pack bottom. I'm now sizing and positioning the pack body box itself.

Adding the flap lid with its hinge at the back edge, then working out strap placement -- realizing the front face is against the torso so straps need to go on the back face instead, with leather strap boxes and brass buckles positioned near the lid's back edge.

But that position conflicts with the gear pouch dimensions, so I'm reconsidering: ditching the vertical back straps and instead wrapping a wide horizontal leather band around the pack body for a cleaner look, which also creates a ledge below the gauges and tools -- repositioning the wrench further left and taller to clear the new band.

For the leather pack color I'm using a patched texture mixing two brown tones for a worn effect. Checking the side pouches, they protrude slightly past the main box edges, and the pipe route near the right side conflicts with the pouch position, so I need to reposition it to avoid overlap.

Instead I'm routing a copper pipe from the gauge bottom down to a small valve wheel, using a curved path with a few control points to give it a natural bend, ending near a torus-shaped handle on the wheel.

Now I'm adding whimsical touches for the gnome tinkerer—goggles instead of a monocle, and a tool belt with pouches hanging at an angle around the waist, positioning each pouch center based on the belt radius and angle offset.

Checking that the pouches don't collide with the arms as they bend down toward the hands, then placing a brass buckle at the belt's front center with tools like a screwdriver sticking out of one pouch for extra character.

Now I'm setting up the module imports needed for the build function—builder, THREE, geometry utilities, glow effects, paint patterns for stripes/patches/mottle/spots—making sure to avoid unused import errors by only including what's actually referenced in the code.

Still writing builder code...

Still defining helper functions...

I'm setting flat shading for the hat facets, then building the spine chain with hips as root and spine/chest joints flowing from a catmull curve, checking that the naming and parenting match the spine role rules before moving to the torso sweep.

Next I'm continuing down the body: neck as a single-joint chain parented to chest, then head attached at the neck's end with its own aim direction, followed by a jaw joint parented to head for facial articulation.

For the face, I'm adding a chin blob and dark mouth cavity both parented to the jaw, then building the head as a larger skin-colored sphere with cheeks, and finishing with white sideburn tufts spiking out from the sides to suggest hair peeking from under a hat.

Now I'm building the arms as symmetric chains looping over left and right sides, defining shoulder-elbow-wrist points, sweeping a tapered shirt-colored mesh along each chain, and computing a hand center point by offsetting from the wrist joint along the arm's direction vector.

Setting up finger and thumb joints off the wrist, then defining capsule shapes for each digit using the glove color and a small tube radius for the segments.

Now I'm working on the leg chain, placing hip, knee, and ankle joints along a polyline parented to the hips, with a contact point near the ankle for ground interaction.

Moving on to the sweep radii for the leg segments and confirming the boots attach to the leg's tip bone, then sketching the SVG textures for the watch dial, starting with the circle rim and stroke outline.

Now I'm adding the needle, center pivot, and tick marks for the dial face, generating the 7 ticks via a loop so stroke widths scale correctly at 192px, and keeping the green gauge arc and transparent background outside the circle intact before moving to the hat texture.

I'm merging small sphere geometries into rivet clusters positioned at the pack corners and along the back band, plus adding brass bolt details to the chest and gear hub, then skipping bib stitching in favor of extruding the bib geometry directly.

Now I'm settling on colors: mustard-brown overalls fabric with a mottled texture for both bib and pants, attached at the chest bone, and starting to plan the shoulder straps extending from the bib's top corners.

Working out strap geometry: merging the backpack's shoulder straps with the overalls straps into leather bands running from the pack top over the shoulders down to the belt, computing torso dome radius and back-of-torso coordinates to position the strap path points accurately.

Still refining strap geometry...

Checking the torso dome radius against strap position to close the gap, then setting torso radii values and strap peak height. I'm also verifying the neck length fits between the torso top and head bottom, and checking that the beard cone placement doesn't awkwardly clash with the bib in front.

Shortening the beard length so its tip sits above the belly instead of overlapping too far down. Then I'm stacking up the hat frustums to compute total figure height, and realizing the sum comes out to about 1.47 meters tall -- way too tall for a gnome, so I need to scale the hat segments down.

Reducing the hat height so the body plus hat lands around 1.35-1.37 meters, which fits the target range of 1-1.4 meters. I'm placing the final pompom sphere at the tip and setting the brim position so it sits above the eyes without covering the face, using a dark red color for the brim.

Positioning the goggles on the hat front, placing the rim and glow lens at the right offset, then treating the hat band itself as the strap so I don't need a separate strap mesh.

Adding a cream pompom at the hat tip, then placing a small flower on the hat band with a stem reaching outward and five petals arranged in a ring facing forward, colored yellow or pink with an orange center. Skipping the mushroom idea and moving on to eyelid details.

Now I'm defining a general frustum-cone helper function that takes a base point, direction, radii, height, color, and bone, which I can reuse for the hat, ears, and beard cones, keeping the mustache sweep thin and tapered with pink cheek blobs added for warmth.

Still working out the beard geometry...

Brow capsule finishes near the brim, good. Now I'm setting up the glow helper and the rig joints — a hinge joint for the lid and a rotor joint for rotation, then building the lid box part with its own bone.

I'm placing strap boxes and a brass buckle on the lid, then checking the lid's flat top against the telescope height — it clears fine at y .84 above the lid's .79. I'm laying out the telescope as three tapering rod segments in brass and steel with an end ring and a teal lens glow.

Now I'm adding the lens detail, a dark eyepiece ring at the back, and small dark brackets mounting the telescope to the chest between the lid and the tube's base, then starting on a spiral spring shape positioned off to the side.

Adding antenna and rotor...

I'm repositioning the small gear to avoid colliding with the band, checking that gear spacing satisfies tooth-radius distance constraints, and verifying the gauge and pipe routing clear the gear assembly geometrically.

Checking the valve-to-wrench overlap, I'm nudging the wrench further left so it doesn't intersect the valve's radius, then setting the wrench's extrusion position, axes, and thickness.

Now I'm positioning the copper pipe near the gears so it clears the front face, then laying out the crank mechanism on the big gear — rod, arm, and knob sphere — checking it doesn't collide with the gauge. Finally I'm cataloging rivet positions at the pack's back corners and the lid corners.

I'm adding more rivets along the band edges and merging all the sphere geometries into one mesh, then building the leather pouches on either side with darker flap overlays and brass snap spheres.

Now for the screwdrivers poking out of the pouch, I'm positioning three angled rods with steel shafts and colored handles (interpolating partway along each rod for the handle segment), using slightly varied tip and base coordinates so they fan out naturally.

Checking the arm and head placements for collisions with the pouch, then moving to the x+ pouch where I'm placing small glowing test tubes with cork stoppers at varied depths, and finally setting up a lantern below with a rope connecting it to the pouch.

Working out the lantern's geometry now — glass body, posts, base, cap cone, and a ring for the rope — plus positioning a steel mug with a torus handle on the opposite side.

Now I'm placing the rope connecting the pouch to the mug and setting up the bedroll as a horizontal cylinder with end bands.

For the legs, I'm thinking about adding whimsical striped socks below the knee, using a color sweep that transitions from the pants color to a cream-and-red striped pattern partway down.

I'm also sketching a small knee patch for the pants—a tiny box with crossed stitch details to give it a mended, lived-in look, while skipping extras like buttons or belt details since the part count is already reasonable at around 150.

Now I'm figuring out the collar: a closed ring swept around the neck at the right height and radius to fit just inside the torso dome, and I'm writing a small helper function to generate ring paths so I can reuse it for the belt and other circular bands.

I'm skipping the scarf and moving to typing details—defining point and vector types, adding optional direction/rotation parameters to the cylinder and blob helpers so they accept either Vector3 or plain number arrays—then starting to write out the full file with the color palette.

For the beard, I'm combining the beard parts into a single surface, scattering tufts across it with minimum distance spacing, and generating card geometry colored off-white with slight lean and spin variation, omitting the bone parameter since the scatter hits already carry the head's weighting. I'm satisfied the double-sided white cards will look fine, and now I'm finishing up by returning the root bone and starting to write the ring path geometry.

I'm generating a closed circular catmull-rom path for the ring shape, then sweeping it into a belt with a small radius and dark leather color, attaching it to the hip joint for rigidity. I'm planning the collar similarly as a closed sweep bound to the neck joint, and setting up the straps with a tapered box-section sweep using a linear radius array for the taper.

For the ellipse radius I'll use a function returning both values instead of a plain array, then move on to writing finger geometry with base and tip positions offset per-finger along the hand direction. I'm double-checking TypeScript strictness concerns like unused variables before writing the final file.
